newsitem.title: USA: Orange County's Citron to work as clerk, avoid jail.
newsitem.headline: Orange County's Citron to work as clerk, avoid jail.

text.p: Former Orange County, Calif., Treasurer Robert Citron, widely blamed for the county's investment crisis, will live at home and serve out his sentence working for the sheriff by day, authorities said.
The Orange County sheriff's department said Citron was assigned Friday to a community work program in lieu of serving time in jail for his role in the county bankruptcy.

Citron will be allowed to live at home. Under the program, he will report to the sheriff's commissary building in Santa Ana, where he will most likely work from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Monday through Friday. He may also have to work some weekends.

His day-to-day duties will include sorting inmate requests for personal items such as envelopes and stamps, alphabetizing and organizing paperwork and handling other clerical jobs, the sheriff's department said.
Citron's first day of work will be Monday. His release date was expected on October 24, 1997, Orange County sheriff spokesman Ron Wilkerson said.

"He's not a violent offender, doesn't pose a threat to the community and he meets all of the requirements of the program," Wilkerson said. But should Citron not follow work program rules, he could be sent to county jail, he added.
About 325 people in Orange County are currently participating in the work program, the department said.

Orange County filed for bankruptcy protection on December 6, 1994 after sustaining losses of more than $1.6 billion on risky investments. It was the largest municipal bankruptcy in U.S. history. The county emerged from bankruptcy in June.
Citron pleaded guilty in April 1995 to six felonies, including counts of making untrue statements in the sale of securities and misusing public funds.
In November, a judge had ordered Citron to spend a year in jail and pay a $100,000 fine for his role in the crisis.
The Orange County district attorney had sought a seven-year prison term and a $400,000 fine for Citron.
